title: Twisted starlight sheds new light on dark matter
excerpt: Scientists discover thousands of cosmic magnifying lenses for exploring the universe
content:
Twisted starlight bent by gravity has been seen across the universe and is helping scientists to uncover the secret of dark matter.

The Euclid telescope has picked up more than 15,000 illuminated arcs and rings created when light travelling from a distant galaxy becomes warped by a large mass of matter in the foreground, creating a cosmic magnifying lens.

The phenomenon, known as gravitational lensing, helps scientists spot areas where dark matter is present – even when it appears invisible – because its significant distorting effect on light can still be seen.

Although no one knows what dark matter is, it is believed to make up about 85 per cent of the universe’s mass, keeping stars and planets in their galaxies.

The search for gravitational lenses was led by University of Portsmouth’s Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, whose team were excited to have found “strong” lenses that occur when large mass sits almost directly in front of a light source.

Natalie Lines, a doctoral researcher at Portsmouth, said: “Strong lensing provides unique insight into the dark universe, allowing us to ‘weigh’ individual galaxies, including their invisible dark matter, and explore how the universe is expanding.

“More than 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery. That day is finally here.”

The £1.2bn Euclid space telescope is led by the European Space Agency (ESA) and is studying the impact of dark matter and dark energy on 1.5 billion galaxies – more than one third of the visible sky, and peering 10 billion years into the past.

The telescope’s enormous field of vision is 250 times larger than the Hubble Space Telescope and creates more data in one day than Hubble has ever produced.

As well as Portsmouth, scientists from University College London, Newcastle, Oxford, Edinburgh, Manchester, Nottingham and the Open University are responsible for many of the instruments on the telescope.

Before Euclid, astronomers had found only a few hundred strong lenses in decades of searching, but the space telescope, which launched in 2023, found 15,000 in its first year of observations.

Dr James Nightingale, an astronomer at Newcastle University, developed the software used to analyse Euclid’s 15,000 strong gravitational lenses.

He said: “When I began studying strong lensing in 2012, I had just 50 lenses to work with. Now, with Euclid, we need to analyse that many every hour just to keep up.

“By doing this for thousands of galaxies, we can begin to answer much bigger questions: how do galaxies grow, where is their matter, and what does this tell us about the universe as a whole?”

As well as the gravitational lenses, the new data release includes images showing more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million quasars, the brilliant cores of distant galaxies, helping astronomers build a detailed 3D map of the cosmos.

“These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos,” said Prof Carole Mundell, the ESA’s director of science.

“This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery in a new regime for astronomy and demonstrating the excellence of European technology, science and international collaboration.”

As well as dark matter, Euclid is also looking for dark energy, which scientists think is responsible for the universe continuing to expand. The idea that the universe is being kept in static equilibrium by an invisible pervading energy was first proposed by Albert Einstein in 1917, who called it the “cosmological constant”.

The telescope could prove Einstein was correct, or usher in an entirely new era of cosmology. 

Prof Andy Taylor, of the University of Edinburgh, said: “These huge, ultra-high-definition images from Euclid are a game-changer for astronomy.

“It is an exciting time for astronomy as we turn these amazing images into a 3D map of the universe, creating a laboratory to probe dark matter and dark energy.”
